title: Branching Strategies
description: Design branching strategies for monorepos, open source, submodules, cross-functional teams, and regulatory environments.

data.text: A branching strategy is the set of conventions your team follows when creating, naming, merging, and deleting branches. Good branching strategies reduce merge conflicts, make code review easier, and align your version-control model with how your organization ships software.
Consistent branch naming is the foundation of a good strategy. Use a prefix to indicate the branch type, followed by a descriptive slug.

Monorepos host multiple services or packages in one repository. Use per-service or per-package directories with scoped feature branches (feature/api/user-search). CI should run only the affected packages, using tools like Nx or Bazel for build scoping.

Maintain a stable main branch. Contributors use short-lived feature branches with pull requests. Maintainers review and squash-merge. No long-lived branches from maintainers. Use labels and milestones to track PR progress.

When using submodules, branching strategies must account for coupled repositories. A change that spans the parent repo and a submodule requires commits in both. Coordinate version bumps across the submodule boundary.

Frontend, backend, and DevOps teams may have different branch lifetimes. Align on an integration cadence (daily or weekly) regardless of individual branch lengths. The team must agree on when branches are eligible for merge.

Highly regulated industries need audit trails and approval chains. Git Flow provides the most explicit structure for this: release branches, mandatory code review, and immutable tags. Document the approval chain in your branching strategy.

data.title: Document and automate your strategy
data.text: Write your branching strategy in CONTRIBUTING.md and enforce it with branch protection rules, CI checks, and commit-lint hooks. Undocumented conventions are followed inconsistently.

items.question: How many long-lived branches should I have?
items.answer: Minimize them. main (or trunk) is always required. develop is common but optional. Release branches are for scheduled-release teams. Every long-lived branch adds merge overhead.

items.question: Should I delete merged branches?
items.answer: Yes, immediately after merging. Set your Git hosting platform to auto-delete branches after merge. Clean branch lists reduce cognitive load.

items.question: How do I handle release branches in trunk-based development?
items.answer: In TBD, you typically do not have long-lived release branches. Instead, you tag releases on main and backport critical fixes as needed.

items.question: What about protected branches?
items.answer: Protect main and any long-lived branches. Require PR reviews, passing CI, and up-to-date branches before merge. This is the most important enforcement mechanism.

data.text: A strategy only works if the tooling enforces it. Branch naming can be validated by a hook or a CI check, branch protection prevents direct pushes to the protected branches, and merge policy decides whether history is linear. The snippets below are the mechanics that turn a documented convention into a rule.

data.title: Enforce a branch-name prefix with a pre-push hook
data.code:
#!/bin/sh
# .git/hooks/pre-push
branch="$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)"
pattern='^(feature|fix|hotfix|release|chore)/[A-Z]+-[0-9]+-[a-z0-9-]+$'

if ! printf '%s' "$branch" | grep -Eq "$pattern"; then
  echo "Branch '$branch' does not match $pattern" >&2
  echo "Example: feature/AUTH-123-login" >&2
  exit 1
fi

data.title: Protect main and choose a merge policy
data.code:
# With the GitHub CLI: require review and passing checks on main
gh api -X PUT repos/:owner/:repo/branches/main/protection \
  -f required_status_checks.strict=true \
  -f required_pull_request_reviews.required_approving_review_count=1 \
  -f enforce_admins=true \
  -f restrictions=null

# Squash-merge keeps main linear while feature branches stay messy
git merge --squash feature/AUTH-123-login
git commit -m "feat(auth): add login endpoint (#482)"

# Or rebase-and-merge for one commit per branch
git rebase origin/main
git switch main
git merge --ff-only feature/AUTH-123-login

data.title: Prefer merge queues when main is hot
data.text: If several pull requests merge per hour, two green branches can still break main when merged together because each was tested against a different main. A merge queue retests each change against the latest main before landing it, which is the difference between a protected branch and a reliable one. Mentioning the merge queue is a strong signal that you have operated this at scale.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use descriptive branch names with consistent prefixes (feature/, fix/, hotfix/)
Minimize long-lived branches — delete them after merging
Monorepos need scoped branching and scoped CI
Regulated environments benefit from Git Flow's explicit audit trail
Document and automate your strategy in CONTRIBUTING.md and CI rules
